mentions.author: veganjay
mentions.text:
I can think of many - I have taken several starting since 2013. The tricky thing is that Coursera classes seem to get merged, re-mashed or otherwise re-branded. And as such only one currently is listed in my "Completed" courses section of my profile.

Having said that and with the caveat that these probably changed since I taken them, I recommend the following:

- Cryptography - [course] - great introduction to the fundamentals and math behind cryptography. A lot of theory but also some practical exercises. This is my top recommended.

- Machine Learning - [course] - a good introduction to the basic of machine learning; focuses on octave/matlab and does not dive into frameworks like…

mentions.author: phyller
mentions.story: Ask HN: What are the best MOOCs you've taken?
mentions.text:
These courses are for beginners, but I started with what I learned from a few courses in Coursera and turned it into a career as a software engineer. [course] and [course] from Jennifer Campbell and Paul Gries from the University of Toronto laid a great foundation to build on. I think I took them the first time they offered it and I still don't understand how they completely nailed a new medium like that first try. It was very accessible, but with enough detail to make sense and the videos were so clear and concise.
The Python one from Rice University, is a fun, awesome course, where you build games to learn. [course]

mentions.author: primitivesuave
mentions.story: Skulpt: client side Python without preprocessing
mentions.text:
Many people, especially kids, will at some point encounter an online learning tool where you can just run Python in the browser. Chances are the underlying interpreter is Skulpt. A short list of examples:

- [link]: has a free online curriculum with more helpful error messages that kids can understand and real-time analytics for teachers

- [link]: handles Python, turtle graphics, and pygal charting in the browser

- [link]: their Python notebook feature uses Skulpt

- [link]: a popular open-source textbook that has excellent Parson's problems

- [link]: implements some custom Skulpt libraries that I haven't seen anywhere else

- [course]: Coursera's interactive Python course

That's just…

mentions.text: I can program (mainly C++, Java, Perl, Ada, SQL) and I had difficulties to improve my weak level in Python because I had (still have) few opportunities to practice.
